summary: BITS Pilani and UNSW authors propose ADFD-Migrate for porting legacy Fortran repositories to Python. An LLM infers an annotated data-flow diagram (processes, data stores, flows, pre/post contracts, and the source files each process covers), and a static-analysis file-coverage check feeds gaps back until 80% of files are covered. The diagram is then split into dependency-ordered chunks for generation, and a name-matching structural diff between the source diagram and one extracted from the generated Python drives regeneration. On the authors' f2x50 benchmark (50 repositories), 327 of 382 author-curated Fortran-oracle probes pass (85.6%), against 21.7% for direct translation. However, on the probes the baselines could actually run, they are about as accurate (83.8-84.7%), so the gain is in how many behaviours get ported at all, not in per-behaviour correctness.

claims.claim: ADFD-Migrate ports pass 327 of 382 Fortran-oracle behavioural probes (85.6%), and 40 of 50 repositories pass every probe
claims.evidence: Table 4, Table D.1 and Tables E.1-E.3. Probes were curated by the authors from public, deterministic routines with small inputs and fixed before porting. There are at least four per repository and many repositories have exactly four. Probes are a lower bound, not system tests (acknowledged). One run per repository at temperature 0.3.

claims.claim: ADFD-Migrate exposes all 382 planned behaviours as runnable targets versus 99/98 for the baselines and 69/30 for the ablations, a 3.9x agreement advantage
claims.evidence: Table 4. Runnable-only agreement is 85.6% for ADFD versus 83.8% (direct) and 84.7% (repository-context), so the advantage is coverage, not correctness. The 382 denominator spans all 50 repositories, but the baselines were run on only 47 (lapack, cp2k and elmerfem were skipped for cost), so those three repositories' 34 probes appear to count as 'non-generated repository' failures for the baselines. The static-profile ablation generates a whole repository from one prompt, and the dependency-chunking ablation scores below plain direct translation (3.7%), which suggests weak ablation implementations. Targets are located by name search plus repository-specific driver adapters.

claims.claim: 93.1% mean migration outcome index and a 17-59 pp outcome-index advantage over direct translation on 47 repositories
claims.evidence: Table 5 (+16.9/+26.6/+58.5 pp by tier) and Table D.2 with bootstrap CIs (+0.270 [0.206, 0.341] vs direct; +0.215 vs repository-context) and Wilcoxon p<0.001. Sensitivity analysis keeps a positive gap in 98.9% of random weightings (Table D.4). However, 60% of the index is an LLM-judged alignment between the source ADFD and an ADFD extracted from each port. ADFD-Migrate explicitly optimises structural alignment to that same ADFD in its loop, and the judge (Opus 4.6) shares a family with the complex-tier generator.

claims.claim: The ADFD workflow lowers cost: about 54% of direct translation on seven complex repositories, with a local 30B model sufficient for the low tier
claims.evidence: App. D.7: $86 vs $159 (direct) and $78 vs $479 (repository-context) on 7 repositories, one run each. Only metered API charges are counted. The cloud-hosted 480B runs are recorded as zero, and local compute and wall time (81-123 min per repository) are not costed.

claims.claim: The explicit ADFD gives developers an inspectable checkpoint where experts can catch defects before generation
claims.evidence: No developer inspected or ratified any ADFD in any reported run (§4.2, App. D.8). The human checkpoint is described but not evaluated.

patterns.note: The recovered ADFD acts as the specification that generation is conditioned on. Against repository-context translation and two no-ADFD ablations on the same 47 repositories and generators, it wins on behaviours delivered and outcome index (bootstrap CIs). The win is in coverage. Per-behaviour correctness ties the baselines where they produce code, and the ablations look under-built.

Making an explicit declarative description of undocumented legacy code before regenerating it is a form of pre-spec discovery. It is fully automated here, and the human review of the recovered description is never exercised.
The ADFD is a machine-readable model with typed I/O and pre/post contracts per process. It is evaluated only as context for code generation, not as domain context that agents or developers consult.

Each ADFD process lists the source files it covers, and coverage scoring checks that every file is linked. Source-target alignment matches names by containment or token Jaccard >= 0.5. These links are checked for presence, not for semantic correctness, and quadpack and roots-fortran show aligned processes with wrong stopping logic.
A static-analysis coverage score drives up to 3-5 re-prompts of ADFD inference. It is not ablated separately (component ablation is listed as future work).
Generation is ordered by SCC/topological chunks of the ADFD process graph. The dependency-chunking ablation uses the call graph but also drops the ADFD content, so graph choice is not isolated.
Human inspectability is claimed as a benefit but not evaluated.
Rule-based Fortran tools (f2py, fable, LFortran) appear only in a feature table and are not run.
Metered API cost is reported for the complex tier only.

methodology.sample: 50 open-source Fortran repositories (20 low / 20 medium / 10 complex; 1.5k-1.6M LoC). Baseline and ablation comparisons use 47 (three largest skipped for cost). 382 author-curated source-oracle probes, at least 4 per repository.
methodology.baselines: Direct file-by-file translation, and repository-context direct translation (prompts reportedly hand-refined). Static-profile ablation: whole repository from one prompt with the static profile. Dependency-chunking ablation: SCC chunks of the call graph. No agentic baseline and no published repository-level translator.
methodology.models: Qwen3-Coder 30B (local Ollama) for the low tier and 4 medium; Qwen3-Coder 480B (cloud) for 16 medium; Claude Sonnet 4.5 for the complex tier. Judge: Claude Opus 4.6. The same generator is used for all methods within a repository; assignment depended on what ADFD-Migrate could complete.
methodology.variance: Single run per repository and method at temperature 0.3. Repository-level bootstrap CIs and Wilcoxon tests on the outcome index only. No run-to-run variance.
methodology.ablations: Two no-ADFD ablations. No ablation of the coverage loop or the alignment-driven regeneration.
methodology.contamination_controls: Repositories selected with no public Python translation. The Fortran sources themselves are public.
methodology.languages: Fortran to Python only; numerical/scientific code

standards.artifacts: f2x50 catalogue and reproduction scripts on GitHub (ShraddhaSurana/iProg); inferred ADFDs, generated Python, metrics and manifests on Zenodo; prompt texts in the replication package

biases.detail: The benchmark, the probes and the composite outcome index were all built by the authors of the system.
60% of the outcome index is alignment to the method's own intermediate representation, which its refinement loop optimises. Another 10% rewards docstrings and type hints.
Semantic alignment is scored by Claude Opus 4.6 with no human validation, and the judge shares a family with the complex-tier generator (acknowledged).
One stochastic run per repository and method. Variance comes from repositories, not from repeated runs.

The static-profile ablation is a single whole-repository prompt, and the dependency-chunking ablation scores below plain direct translation. The three repositories skipped for cost appear to count as baseline failures in the 382-probe denominator.
One language pair with a Python target. Import reconciliation is Python-specific. The authors note that event-driven or I/O-heavy code may benefit less.
The 'representative' repository comparisons in Table D.3 all show large gains.
Cost counts only metered API charges, so local and cloud Ollama compute is treated as free.

coi.affiliations: BITS Pilani K. K. Birla Goa Campus (India); UNSW Sydney (Australia)
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Third-party models (Qwen3-Coder, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6); the authors' own method and benchmark
coi.funding: No specific grant; competing interests declared none
coi.detail: Academic authors evaluating their own method on their own benchmark (counted as a bias, not a COI). There is no vendor tie.

verdict_reason: It uses real repositories of wide size range, probes fixed before porting and run against the original Fortran, two ablations, bootstrap CIs and released artifacts. Against that: single runs, author-curated probes, a composite metric tilted toward the method's own representation, and weak ablations. The paper's own Table 4 shows the gain is in coverage (more behaviours delivered), not in per-behaviour correctness. Relevance to the discovery scope is indirect.
applicability: The transferable idea for the Java team is a recovered, machine-checkable design model of undocumented code: processes, data stores, flows and contracts, each linked to the files it covers. Deterministic static analysis checks that every module is represented before anything is generated. That is a candidate pre-spec discovery and onboarding artifact for the 4+ ingestion repositories. The evidence is for Fortran-to-Python porting of numerical libraries where data flow dominates. The team's ingestion services are I/O- and event-heavy, which the authors expect to benefit less. The human-review step, which is the part that would help new developers, was never exercised. File-level coverage proves only that a module is mentioned, not that its description is right. Treat this as a design idea, for example checking an agent-written architecture summary against a static module inventory, and not as evidence of correctness gains.
